R0085.title: Ransomware Attack
R0085.definition: The potential threat where attackers encrypt victims' data or threaten to expose their sensitive information, then demand ransom payment to unlock or withhold the data.
R0085.description: Scenarios include using malware to infect systems, encrypting files, and then extorting victims to pay for decryption keys or to prevent information leakage.
R0085.influence: Harms include data loss, system paralysis, and business disruption, potentially causing enormous financial losses, reputational damage, and legal liability for organizations.

references.title: T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact - MITRE ATT&CK

observables: Server files are encrypted in bulk and renamed with anomalous extensions such as .locked/.encrypted
A large number of files are renamed within a short window, while volume shadow copies and backup services are disabled or deleted
Lateral movement traffic surges on the internal network, with anomalous SMB/RDP connections and PsExec/WMI remote execution
Ransom note files (such as README / How-to-decrypt.txt) appear simultaneously across multiple directories
Large-scale data exfiltration traffic appears before encryption, uploading to unknown external storage during off-hours

R0085-001.title: Ransomware as a Service (RaaS)
R0085-001.definition: Ransomware as a Service is a criminal business model where ransomware developers provide ransomware tools and infrastructure as a service to other criminals, sharing a percentage of the ransom.
R0085-001.description: The RaaS model significantly lowers the technical barrier for ransomware attacks, enabling criminals without technical skills to launch ransomware attacks. RaaS platforms typically provide: ransomware generators, encryption/decryption tools, ransom negotiation platforms, victim management panels, and technical support services. Well-known RaaS groups include LockBit, BlackCat/ALPHV, and Cl0p. The typical RaaS business model has developers taking 20%-30% of the ransom as a platform fee, with the remainder going to the 'affiliates' who actually launch the attacks.
R0085-001.influence: The number and frequency of ransomware attacks increase significantly, small and medium enterprises become primary targets, and ransom amounts continue to rise.

references.title: Ransomware as a Service Trend Analysis

observables: Ransomware samples match signatures of known RaaS families (LockBit/BlackCat/Cl0p)
Ransom negotiation pages show common RaaS platform templates and ransom payment addresses
The initial access techniques used by affiliate accounts align with the RaaS division-of-labor model
Multiple victims are hit by the same ransomware family but the attack source IPs/infrastructure differ
The dark web leak site publishes victim data batch-listed by the RaaS platform

R0085-002.title: Double / Triple Extortion
R0085-002.definition: In addition to encrypting data, attackers add data leakage threats (double extortion) and pressure on the victim's customers/partners (triple extortion) as multiple extortion tactics.
R0085-002.description: Double/triple extortion is an escalated form of ransomware attack (R0085). (1) Double extortion: attackers steal a copy of the victim's data before encrypting it, threatening to publicly leak the data on the dark web if the victim refuses to pay. (2) Triple extortion: in addition to double extortion, attackers also contact the victim's customers, partners, or regulators to notify them of the data breach, applying additional pressure to force payment. (3) Quadruple extortion: some attackers also simultaneously launch DDoS attacks to further paralyze the victim's business systems. This multi-extortion strategy means that even comprehensive data backups cannot fully mitigate ransomware risk.
R0085-002.influence: Data leakage risk persists even with backups, customer and partner trust is damaged, and compliance penalty risks arise.

observables: Large-scale data exfiltration traffic appears before encryption, indicating data was stolen beforehand
The dark web leak site publishes victim enterprise data samples as extortion leverage
Attackers proactively contact the victim's customers, partners, or regulators to apply pressure
Ransom notes contain data leakage threats and a public disclosure countdown page
The same incident is accompanied by DDoS attacks that further paralyze business systems
